shortDescription: A practical walkthrough for building rubrics that make grading faster and feedback clearer.
body:
A good rubric does two jobs at once: it speeds up your grading and it shows students exactly what quality work looks like before they submit.

This guide walks through criteria selection, performance level descriptions, and common pitfalls like overly vague language or too many dimensions.
author: Kristina Maricle

resourceTitle: AI in the Classroom: Getting Started
shortDescription: A pedagogical (not technical) primer on deciding what role AI tools should play in your course.
body:
Before writing an AI policy, it helps to decide what you actually want students to practice and produce in your course.

This post offers a framework for thinking through where AI use supports your learning objectives and where it short-circuits them.
author: Morgan Vickery

resourceTitle: Keynote Recording: Building a Culture of Care
shortDescription: Full recording of the Fall 2025 Teaching Conference keynote on care-centered course design.
body:
Our Fall 2025 Teaching Conference keynote explored what it means to design courses where students feel seen and supported without lowering academic expectations.

The recording runs about 50 minutes including audience Q&A.
author: Dr. Elena Vasquez, Keynote Speaker

shortDescription: A downloadable syllabus starting point with accessible formatting and suggested policy language.
body:
This template includes suggested language for attendance, communication expectations, and how students can access course materials.

Every section is editable; delete what does not fit your course and make the language your own.
author: Heather Hammond

shortDescription: How to turn vague course goals into objectives you can actually teach toward and assess.
body:
Understand and appreciate are goals, not objectives. This guide covers verbs that describe observable performance and how to align objectives with assessments.

Includes worked examples from courses across disciplines.
citations:
• Wiggins, G. & McTighe, J. (2005). Understanding by Design. ASCD.
  • Anderson, L. & Krathwohl, D. (2001). A Taxonomy for Learning, Teaching, and Assessing. Longman.
author: Lisa Sieg

shortDescription: Slides from our workshop on structuring group work students do not dread.
body:
These slides cover role assignment, individual accountability within group grades, and activity structures that make collaboration feel purposeful.

Presented at the Spring 2026 workshop series.
author: Kristina Maricle

shortDescription: Five low-prep techniques for finding out what students actually understand before the exam does.
body:
Formative assessment does not require new grading burden. Muddiest point, one-minute papers, and confidence polling all take minutes to run.

This post explains when each technique fits and what to do with what you learn.
author: Lisa Sieg

shortDescription: How to evaluate OER for quality and fit, and where to find materials in your discipline.
body:
Open educational resources can remove real cost barriers for students, but evaluating quality takes a practiced eye.

This guide covers the major OER repositories, licensing basics, and a rubric for evaluating fit with your course.
author: Morgan Vickery

shortDescription: Recording of our hands-on workshop applying UDL principles to real course materials.
body:
Participants brought their own assignments and syllabi and revised them live using Universal Design for Learning principles.

The recording includes the full working session and the debrief discussion.
author: Kristina Maricle

shortDescription: Rethinking attendance requirements so they encourage presence without punishing crisis.
body:
Strict attendance policies often punish exactly the students who most need flexibility, while doing little to motivate the rest.

This post explores policy designs that communicate that showing up matters while leaving room for life to happen.
author: Jennifer Hall

shortDescription: A semester-at-a-glance planning template for sequencing content, assessments, and workload.
body:
Seeing the whole semester on one page makes it much easier to spot workload pile-ups and pacing problems before students do.

Download the template and fill in your topics, due dates, and your own grading load week by week.
author: Heather Hammond

resourceTitle: Grading for Growth: Making Resubmission Work
shortDescription: How to offer revision and resubmission without doubling your grading load.
body:
Resubmission policies signal that learning matters more than first attempts, but they collapse without clear structure.

This guide covers eligibility rules, revision memos, and grading shortcuts that keep resubmission sustainable for you.
citations: • Clark, D. & Talbert, R. (2023). Grading for Growth. Routledge.
author: Lisa Sieg

shortDescription: Slides from the spring demo session on classroom polling and collaborative annotation tools.
body: A quick tour of the interactive tools demonstrated at the spring session, with pedagogical use cases for each.
author: Morgan Vickery

shortDescription: Collecting student feedback while there is still time to act on it, and closing the loop.
body:
End-of-semester course evals arrive too late to help the students who wrote them. Mid-semester feedback fixes the timing problem.

This guide covers lightweight collection methods and, crucially, how to respond to what you hear so students know it mattered.
author: Kristina Maricle
